segments.text: Listing part B. You hear a doctor talking to the daughter of a patient from an aged care home. Now read the question.
Hello Mrs Cox, come on in and sit down.
Oh thank you.
How are you today?
Oh fine thanks.
And how's your father doing since we last spoke?
Oh up and down.
I'm still finding he seems to be getting increasingly forgetful.
he confuses easily and this makes him really frustrated. Right so as you remember from last
time we did a range of tests on your father and based on those results it does look like he's
developed an early onset Alzheimer's disease so that would probably account for his memory loss
his feelings of hopelessness and his anger at times as well.
What do you think the next step is then?
We can't do a lot about his memory,
but we can help him to change his mood and enjoy life more.
There's some good medications around
and that may slow the deterioration.
I think it's important that he goes back to the aged care home
and find some enjoyment in the activities that they do.
It's difficult to determine the long-term outlook,
but we'll start him on the medication
and we'll check on him again in a couple of weeks
to see how he's going.
Okay, thank you, Doctor.
I'm grateful for all your help.
Listening Part B.
You hear a consultant giving a talk to a group of trainees.
Now read the question.
The first 24 hours after a head injury are the most important, although after effects
may appear much later.
It's important that the patient is woken every 2 hours for the first 24 hours.
If they're recovering at home, then this should be by someone responsible, who is able to
also watch for the following symptoms.
Persistent headache, nausea or vomiting.
Weakness, numbness or paralysis of the arms or legs.
Blood or clear fluid coming from the ears or nose.
Blurred vision or one pupil larger than the other.
And convulsions.
If any of these occur, then the person will need to call their GP immediately or return
to the hospital emergency department.
Listening Part B. You hear a vet talking to a client who brought his pet cat Jimmy to
the vet clinic.
Now read the question.
Okay, the examination has revealed large amounts of struvite crystals in Jimmy's urethra.
So that's why he's had difficulty urinating.
The good news is that there's no bladder stones and no major blockages.
Oh, that's good.
And his kidneys are fine, so there's no evidence of damage.
That's great.
Yeah, but I need you to understand that this condition is very painful and distressing for Jimmy.
Okay, right.
So, it's certainly a significant problem at the moment, and he'll continue experiencing difficulty in urinating.
And for male cats in particular, there is a risk of developing a urethral obstruction, which can be fatal.
How do you make sure that doesn't happen then?
Well, we can make some dietary changes, which will definitely help.
but I'd also like to know if Jimmy's been feeling stressed at all lately.
Have there been any changes in his living environment?
Well, we have been doing upper house at the moment.
Ah, that could do it.
Stress is definitely a contributing factor with this condition.
Listening Part B.
You hear the nurse unit manager discussing the progress of a patient
at a multidisciplinary team meeting.
Now read the question.
Now on to Margaret Smith.
She's a 68-year-old woman who was brought into ED two days ago
by her son, Jeff.
Margaret was diagnosed four years ago with frontotemporal lobar degeneration
and has progressively deteriorated in that time
She also has hypertension and depression
Her GP recently started her on an antidepressant medication
She lives at home with her son, who's her sole full-time carer
but nursing staff have been unable to contact him since her admission to hospital
Margaret's shown changes in her social behaviour recently
She's been declining food at home and on the ward the nurses have reported she's holding
food in her mouth.
She's refusing to take medication.
She's been very agitated on the ward and she's yelling out when nursing staff try and assist
her and she's been confused and physically aggressive on occasion.
She's also calling out regularly for her son.
Listening Part B. You hear a radiographer talking to nursing staff at an aged care centre.
Now read the question.
The most important preparation requirements include obtaining a recent EGFR result and
providing details of current prescriptions, over-the-counter medications and information
on pregnancy status.
Please also ensure that patients follow a hydration fast for four hours prior to examination.
Patients with a recent history of fever, diarrhoea and dialysis are not suitable to undergo CT scans with contrast use.
The examination takes between 10 and 45 minutes depending on the procedure type and possible side effects include nausea, vomiting and dizziness.
The CT contrast usually stays in the patient's system 48 hours after the injection and following
the examination I recommend advising patients to drink plenty of extra water as this encourages
secretion of the CT contrast media. Finally if any complications such as allergic reactions,
decreased urine output, confusion or blood in urine occur then please inform your patients
to let medical staff know as soon as possible.
Listening part B. You hear a GP discussing psoriasis with a patient. Now read the question.
You've got something called chronic plaque psoriasis on your elbows and knees, but don't
worry, we can treat it.
You definitely benefit from some light treatment to help your rash settle down.
I'd recommend coming up to the physiotherapy department twice a week to have UVB light treatment.
Are you arranging me to have sunbed treatment, Doctor?
Well, there are some similarities to sunbed treatment,
but actually the lights that we have in hospital are special and they admit only a UVB light.
You will get a suntan though.
Sounds great. When can I start?
There's a bit of a waiting list, so I'll give you this cream to be getting on with first.
take the form to the physiotherapy department and they'll book you in for
six weeks of UBB treatment. All the best then. Thank you.
